newsitem.title: CHINA: FEATURE-HK torn over heartbreak child deportations.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-HK torn over heartbreak child deportations.

text.p: Just after Asia's "party of the century" to mark a return to Chinese rule, Hong Kong faces classic heartbreak over forcibly separated families.
In its first major controversial decision, a new China-appointed Provisional Legislature has enacted a tough law to send illegal child immigrants back to mainland China.

The law could mean deportation of thousands of Chinese, mainly children, who over the last few years have sneaked or been smuggled into Hong Kong, a British colony until it reverted to China on July 1.

It also affects some 66,000 children on the mainland who, by virtue of having parents already permanently resident in Hong Kong, have residency rights under the Basic Law, Hong Kong's new mini-constitution.

At the heart of the controversial new law is a requirement for would-be immigrants to secure "certificates of entitlement" before entering Hong Kong. This means children already in Hong Kong may be deported even if they are entitled to come and settle.
HEARTBREAK FOR SEPARATED FAMILIES
"You may treat some people as precious gold, but they treat you like worthless straw," goes an old Chinese adage.
And for the tens of thousands of young children in mainland China, and their parents in Hong Kong, these broken-hearted separated families are finding the old saying sadly true.
The Hong Kong government has said that the new law is needed to ensure that mainland people coming to settle in Hong Kong do so in an orderly fashion.

A poll carried out by Hong Kong University showed 78 percent of people agreed with the new law's provision that mainland-born children secure relevant documents before coming to Hong Kong. Only 9.5 percent disagreed.
Almost 80 percent of the 538 people polled thought those who had jumped the queue should first be repatriated.

Local newspapers also gave the law a thumbs-up. "These children were not stripped of their right to live in Hong Kong," said the pro-Beijing Ta Kung Pao. "They should come to Hong Kong by legal means and in an orderly manner."
The Sing Tao daily urged authorities in Hong Kong and southern China to step up border patrols to prevent mainland children from sneaking in.
MANY IN HONG KONG STARTED AS REFUGEES
For decades Hong Kong has given shelter to hundreds of thousands of Chinese refugees and immigrants, as well as Vietnamese boatpeople fleeing their country's communist regime.

Hundreds of thousands of Chinese fled to Hong Kong, notably in the 1950s and 1960s, to escape communist crackdowns and political mayhem on the mainland. To many Chinese, Hong Kong is a capitalist paradise.
Hong Kong's new Beijing-installed leader, Tung Chee-hwa, was himself a refugee from the mainland after the 1949 communist takeover.
Many of these former refugees and economic migrants now complain that new arrivals are sapping scarce housing, education and welfare resources.
A Hong Kong immigration spokesman said the department regularly repatriates illegal immigrants including children. It has deported an average of eight persons a day so far this month.
DOES NEW LAW VIOLATE "CONSTITUTIONAL" RIGHTS?
The law drew attack from legal experts and human rights groups who said it violates Hong Kong's "mini-constitution."
Law professor Nihal Jayawickrama said the bill violated the Basic Law, which gives children the legal right to join parents who already are permanent residents.
"What's happening here is that the fundamental law of Hong Kong, the Basic Law, is being infringed right from the beginning," Jayawickrama said.
"Under the Basic Law, this category of people have been given rights, the right of abode...you don't commit an offence by entering your home country," he said.
"It's illogical and for Hong Kong people, it sends the message that your constitutional rights are not worth very much," said human rights lawyer Rob Brooks.
But for the families of mainland-born children already here, there is no backing down. Some are preparing to sue the Hong Kong government for violating the Basic Law.

They have also applied for legal aid to mount a court challenge to the legality of their deportation and about 50 have been successful, clearing the way for them to take on the government in court. More than 100 lawyers have offered free service to help children who fail to get legal aid.
